title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Aviation
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Check Point firewalls are being exploited through the VPN handshake, and a separate management-server flaw was in use two months before a fix — both entered KEV on 22 September
items.content_text: Check Point published a security advisory on 22 September confirming active exploitation of two separate critical flaws, both rated CVSS 9.8. The first, CVE-2026-85102, is in Security Gateways and Spark firewalls: improper validation of certificate data during VPN negotiation lets an unauthenticated attacker execute code on the gateway. Check Point released the fix on 9 September and writes that “starting September 12, 2026, we observed a wave of exploitation attempts against Spark customers”; it gives no customer count and no attribution, and publishes indicators in the form of exploitation certificates with the subjects CN=vpn, CN=vpn-user or CN=vpnuser, OU=users, O=global. The second, CVE-2026-93616, is a pre-authentication path traversal in the Security Management web service that leads to script execution or Java class loading. Check Point says it was used in “a handful of pinpointed attacks on July 23, 2026”, about two months before the fix became available on 22 September. It is not CVE-2026-91843, the earlier management-server username flaw, which is still not reported as exploited. CISA added both flaws to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 22 September with a federal deadline of 25 September, in the same batch as Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator and F5 BIG-IP APM. That deadline arrived on 25 September; Check Point’s advisory carried no further update notes as of this edition, and no new exploitation details have been published. No airport, airline or air navigation service provider has been named as a victim. The story leads this page because Check Point is the most widely deployed product under confirmed exploitation this week, and because of where it sits in aviation. Spark is Check Point’s small-office firewall line, the class of appliance fitted at outlying sites such as NAVAID and radar shelters, fuel farms, cargo sheds and contractor offices, and often run by a managed-service provider. Check Point gateways also terminate the remote-access VPNs that integrators use to reach terminal BMS, baggage and airfield-lighting systems. The management server is the bigger prize, because it holds the policy for every gateway it manages.

items.title: UK air traffic failure traced to a software defect in aircraft code allocation — NATS’ preliminary report describes a timing fault, not an attack
items.content_text: This is not a cyber incident. It is carried here, clearly labelled, because it is the aviation infrastructure story of the period and readers will reasonably have wondered. On 8 September a failure at NATS, the UK air navigation service provider, forced Heathrow to suspend arrivals and disrupted Gatwick and Manchester, affecting more than 2,000 flights across 8–9 September. NATS’ preliminary report, published on 18 September, places the cause in a small part of the National Airspace System: a software defect in the code that allocates aircraft identification codes. A code request was paused when a higher-priority task pre-empted it, and the update did not complete; Reuters quotes the report as saying that had the higher-priority request arrived “even one millisecond earlier or later, the update would have completed normally.” Restrictions lasted about six hours and clearing the backlog took more than two days. NATS says a mitigation is in place while a permanent fix is safety-tested and deployed. Chief executive Martin Rolfe, who had already ruled out cyber on 10 September, dismissed speculation of military interference and said the fault is unrelated to the 2023 outage; the early accounts blaming an anomalous military flight plan are not supported by the stated cause. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander called the failure “completely unacceptable” and has tasked the Civil Aviation Authority with an independent review of NATS’ findings, its resilience investment plans and regulatory accountability. A full report is to follow, and NATS proposes a further £1bn of investment by 2033. For aviation OT teams the lesson is availability engineering rather than attack defence: a defect that only surfaces when two tasks collide within a millisecond is exactly the kind of fault conventional testing can miss, so the useful questions are how your own flight-critical systems behave when an update stalls and how quickly you recover when one does. Addendum, 21 September: FlightGlobal reports that a separate “connectivity” issue at NATS’ Prestwick centre in Scotland caused delays at several airports less than two weeks after the 8 September failure. No cause has been published, NATS has not linked it to the earlier defect, and nothing in the reporting suggests a cyber element. We carry it as an unattributed operational fault and will update if NATS publishes a cause.

items.title: Berlin Brandenburg stops all flying for 45 minutes on a drone sighting, its 28th drone this year against eight in all of 2025 — the gap is detection, not defence
items.content_text: On the evening of Wednesday 23 September, Germany’s air navigation service DFS closed Berlin Brandenburg’s northern runway after a drone was sighted at about 20:00 local time. It closed the southern runway at 20:20 and lifted the closure at 21:05, dpa reports, leaving the airport with no take-offs or landings for about 45 minutes. Numerous flights were delayed and several were diverted. The Federal Police searched and found nothing, and Brandenburg police have opened an investigation into dangerous interference with air traffic. No operator or motive has been identified. Some early English-language reports gave the closure as about five minutes, apparently misreading the time zone; dpa’s timeline gives 45. The trend matters more than the single event. DFS figures reported by dpa put drones recorded at BER at 28 in the first half of 2026, against eight in the whole of 2025, and flying was suspended seven times in the half-year. Earlier in the month, Brussels Airport halted traffic for roughly half an hour on the evening of Friday 12 September after a drone was sighted near the airfield; no injuries or damage were reported and movements resumed once the area was cleared, with the drone’s origin and intent unattributed. The following day Vilnius closed for 38 minutes on a drone alert that scrambled a NATO jet before the object was confirmed to be a flock of birds. Both follow the US Labor Day weekend incursion at San Diego that grounded around 400 flights, where the TSA reportedly could not identify the operator and coverage noted that US airports carry no mandatory drone-detection requirement at all. None of this is a cyberattack and none of it should be filed as one. It belongs on this page because the operational consequence is identical to an OT failure and lands on the same people: a ground stop cascades into stand and gate reallocation, jet-bridge and ramp re-sequencing, baggage re-flow and fuel and de-icing re-planning, and the decision to stop or resume is increasingly taken from software — counter-UAS detection feeds, ground-movement displays, airfield lighting control — that few airports treat as operational technology with an integrity requirement. Vilnius is the instructive one: the cost was not the drone, it was the ambiguity.

items.title: A China-linked crew is emptying self-hosted code repositories of SCADA and HMI source — and aerospace is on the victim list
items.content_text: Acronis threat intelligence, published on 13 September and reported on 14–15 September, describes a campaign it attributes with moderate confidence to a China-linked actor it calls Red Heron, exploiting a critical remote code execution flaw in the self-hosted Gitea code platform, CVE-2026-60004, since 29 July. The actor scanned 1,386 internet-facing Gitea instances across seven countries and compromised 11 organisations in five countries, by Acronis’s count (some secondary reports give higher figures) — the victim set spanning aerospace, telecommunications, government, elections and defence alongside industry. Two victims define the objective: a Taiwanese industrial-automation company whose stolen repositories covered SCADA and HMI tooling, IoT platform integrations and network-sniffer products, and a Canadian renewable-energy firm from which infrastructure maps, configuration secrets, SSH host keys and internal tokens were taken. The implant, a custom loader Acronis calls JITTERLY with an embedded Linux rootkit named SIXZUT, supports more than thirty post-exploitation commands. Nothing here is aviation-specific and no airport or airline has been named, but the pattern is the one that reaches this sector indirectly: MRO software houses, baggage and BMS integrators and ground-systems developers routinely keep deployment configurations, VPN profiles, device credentials and site diagrams in self-hosted repositories that sit outside anyone’s OT security programme. Stolen host keys and infrastructure maps are not the attack; they are the preparation for one that arrives later looking like legitimate maintenance access. On 21 September GreyNoise reported that the actor behind the Zyxel GS1900 switch campaign also targeted Gitea CVE-2026-60004, and it infers an overlap with Red Heron from shared command-and-control and malware; that is GreyNoise’s inference, not Acronis’s finding, and we carry it as such.

items.title: GAO: the FAA cannot see spectrum attacks on aircraft communications in real time, and the ACARS and CPDLC datalinks could carry a forged clearance
items.content_text: The US Government Accountability Office published GAO-26-108439 on 21 September, titled “Aviation Cybersecurity: Enhanced Air Safety Requires FAA to Better Mitigate Threats to Aircraft Communications.” Auditors examined the text-based datalinks that carry messages between aircraft, airline operations and air traffic control — ACARS and Controller-Pilot Data Link Communications — and found weaknesses in authentication, encryption and protocol design such that, in GAO’s words, “a malicious actor could transmit fraudulent clearance cancellations, possibly leading to flight delays or safety issues.” On the spectrum side, GAO found that the FAA acknowledges jamming and spoofing as threats but “did not have a defined, real-time monitoring and detection capability for all spectrum-related threats,” and that its risk assessments and security documentation for the National Airspace System are incomplete. GAO makes nine recommendations, covering NAS risk assessments, real-time spectrum-threat monitoring, interagency coordination and stronger authentication and encryption for aircraft communications; the Department of Transportation concurred with all nine, and all nine were open at publication. This is an audit, not an incident. GAO reports no exploitation of either weakness; the report is carried because it is the most substantive primary-source aviation item of the fortnight, not because anything happened. It matters to this page for two reasons. The datalink finding belongs to airlines and their communications providers, and it puts on the record that a message channel crews act on is not authenticated. The spectrum finding is the same problem the Jammertest work exposed for GNSS, stated at national scale: a signal that is manipulated rather than removed produces no alarm anywhere in the chain, and nobody currently owns detecting it.

items.title: Norway spent forty minutes convincing a rescue helicopter it was somewhere else — and the avionics never reported a fault
items.content_text: At Jammertest 2026, the annual open interference exercise on Andøya, researchers escalated a spoofing signal on 10 September until a rescue helicopter’s GPS display showed a false position out over the Norwegian Sea and a track of tight overlapping turns, while the aircraft in fact flew normally. The finding worth carrying is the detection asymmetry rather than the spectacle: jamming announces itself as signal loss and crews are trained for it, whereas spoofing leaves the receiver confidently reporting data that is internally consistent, plausible and wrong. This was a controlled test, not an in-the-wild incident, and no aircraft was endangered. It lands against a real backdrop the researchers cited — RAF aircraft encountering GPS jamming near the Russian border and daily GNSS interference over Sweden through 2026 — and it reinforces the updated jamming and spoofing guidance EASA issued to operators in July 2026. For airport operators the read-across runs past the flight deck. GNSS is not only a navigation input; it is a cheap and widely deployed time source, and GNSS-disciplined clocks quietly underpin surveillance feeds, surface-movement and logging across ground estates. A time source that can be walked rather than broken is a category of failure most airport OT inventories have never recorded. One defensive development came out of the same exercise: Splash247 reported on 17 September that ESA tested Galileo’s Signal Authentication Service (SAS), working alongside OSNMA, during Jammertest. Five operational Galileo satellites broadcast encrypted signals for two hours; under spoofing, conventional receivers reported false positions while SAS-equipped receivers detected the interference. Further testing and accreditation come first, and the initial service — free and worldwide — is due in 2027, so this belongs on the receiver roadmap rather than in today’s mitigation.
tags: Research — GNSS spoofing against airborne receivers; controlled exercise, not an attack

items.title: August set a global ransomware record at 997 attacks, with utilities among the categories driving the rise
items.content_text: Comparitech data reported on 14 September recorded 997 ransomware attacks worldwide in August 2026 — an average of 32 a day, a 23 percent increase on July’s 809, and above the previous monthly record of 988. The reporting singles out utility, healthcare and business-services attacks as the categories behind the surge. Treat the absolute number with the usual caution — counts of this kind depend on leak-site claims and disclosure practice as much as on actual incident volume, and claimed victims are not confirmed victims. The direction of travel, however, is consistent with what operators are seeing. Airlines, airports and their service providers sit inside the business-services and transport categories driving this figure. Aviation's recent history is consistent: the encryption lands on a shared IT provider or a back-office system, and the visible failure is at check-in, baggage or turnaround rather than in a control system.

items.title: Cyber-informed engineering argues the useful question is not how to keep attackers out, but which consequences you can design away
items.content_text: An analysis published 15 September sets out the case for cyber-informed engineering in critical infrastructure: that industrial systems operate under a constraint IT does not share, because a compromised network does not automatically have to become a catastrophic physical event. The argument is to move the security question upstream into design — identifying the physical consequences that actually matter, then engineering them out with controls that do not depend on the digital system remaining trustworthy. Aviation's safety culture already embeds the principle — independent systems, engineered fallbacks, defined degraded modes. The argument here is to apply it explicitly to airport and airline OT, asking where a network compromise could produce a physical or safety consequence and what design change would remove that possibility. This is practitioner analysis rather than incident reporting; it names no victim and describes no attack, but it is the most useful lens available for operators whose detection budget will never match their consequence exposure.

items.title: Arista’s VeloCloud SD-WAN orchestrator has a CVSS 10 flaw under active attack — the console that configures the links to your outlying sites
items.content_text: Arista published Security Advisory 0183 on 22 September for CVE-2026-93952, an improper input validation flaw in on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO), rated CVSS 10.0 under v3.1 and 9.5 under v4.0. Arista says the flaw “may allow a remote attacker to access privileged internal functionality and impact the VCO host” and that it is “known to be actively exploited.” Exposure depends on configuration. An attacker needs certificate-based authentication to be set up between VeloCloud Edges and the orchestrator, the public part of an Edge’s authentication certificate, and network access to the VCO web interface; “VCO tenant or operator credentials are not required.” Vulnerable on-prem releases are 5.2.3.15 and earlier, 6.1.3.7 and earlier, 6.4.2.7 and earlier, and 7.0.0.2 and earlier. Fixes are in 5.2.3.16 and 6.4.2.8, and Arista lists no fixed build yet for the 6.1 or 7.0 trains. Hosted and dedicated VCO instances have already been patched. Arista publishes indicators: the files /usr/local/sbin/.vcnode.js and /usr/local/sbin/vc-sysmond (MD5 dc78e206eaeadec59fc5801fe4556bd0), a vc-sysmon systemd service, an x-vc-opt HTTP header, and the source addresses 142.93.149.77 and 104.248.126.159. CISA added the flaw to KEV on 22 September with a 25 September deadline. No aviation victim is named. The aviation angle is architectural. An SD-WAN orchestrator pushes configuration and policy to every edge it manages, and those edges can connect remote NAVAID and surveillance sites, fuel farms, cargo and MRO facilities, and regional airports to the core network. Compromising the orchestrator gives an attacker a view of every site and possibly a way into each one.

items.title: An F5 BIG-IP APM overflow gives unauthenticated code execution, but only where APM acts as an OAuth authorisation server — and it is being exploited
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-94127 in F5 BIG-IP Access Policy Manager to the KEV catalog on 22 September, with a federal deadline of 25 September. The flaw is a heap-based buffer overflow rated CVSS 9.8 that allows unauthenticated remote code execution. It is covered by F5 advisory K000162605. Exposure is narrower than the score suggests. Rapid7’s analysis says a system is exposed only when a virtual server has both an APM access policy and an OAuth profile attached, so that APM is acting as an OAuth authorisation server. F5 has issued engineering hotfixes for the 21.1.0, 17.5.0 and 17.1.0 branches. Rapid7 reported no confirmed public proof-of-concept as of 22 September, and F5 has published no attribution or victim count. No aviation victim is named. It belongs on this page because BIG-IP APM is widely used as the access gateway in front of web portals and vendor remote access, the role it can play for crew, engineering and MRO applications and for integrator access into airport systems, and in an OAuth-server role it issues the tokens those applications trust.

items.title: Cisco’s network access control server has a CVSS 10 authentication bypass under active attack — this is the box that decides which devices get onto which airport network
items.content_text: Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 on 16 September for CVE-2026-76460, a CVSS 10.0 flaw in Identity Services Engine and ISE-PIC that lets an unauthenticated remote attacker bypass the web-based management interface through an API endpoint with insufficient authentication. Cisco states its PSIRT “is aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability.” All versions are affected; fixes are 3.1 Patch 12, 3.2 Patch 11, 3.3 Patch 12, 3.4 Patch 7 and 3.5 Patch 4. There are no workarounds — restricting management traffic with infrastructure access control lists is the only mitigation short of patching. CISA added the CVE to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 16 September with an unusually short three-day federal remediation deadline of 19 September, which has now passed. No attribution has been published and no critical-infrastructure or aviation targeting has been claimed; Singapore’s Cyber Security Agency issued its own alert on 21 September urging immediate patching. The reason it matters here is architectural rather than reported: where an airport or airline estate runs 802.1X and posture-based access control, ISE is the policy engine that decides which contractor laptop, handheld or engineering workstation lands on a terminal, baggage or airside VLAN — so administrative control of it is control of the segmentation itself.

items.title: A Zyxel small-office switch flaw enters KEV after 996 devices in 48 countries were harvested for configurations and credentials — the kit in the corners of an airport nobody inventories
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 21 September with a federal remediation deadline of 24 September. The flaw is a stack-based buffer overflow in the CGI program of Zyxel’s GS1900-series managed switches — GS1900-8, 8HP, 10HP, 16, 24, 24E, 24EP, 24HPv2, 48 and 48HPv2 — that lets an unauthenticated attacker on the LAN execute operating-system commands with a crafted HTTP request; Zyxel patched it on 16 June in firmware 2.90(AAHH.2)C0 and per-model equivalents, and publishes no CVSS score for it. GreyNoise’s report of the same day documents what it describes as the first in-the-wild exploitation: a single actor, active since 7 May and assessed as a Chinese speaker, compromised 996 GS1900 switches across 48 countries — Italy, the United States, Taiwan, France, South Korea and the Netherlands lead the count — using an obfuscated Python tool that pulled device configurations and root-level hashed credentials over TFTP; 564 of the victims were still on factory-default credentials. The same actor stole records from an unnamed western government organisation through two WordPress flaws and also targeted Gitea CVE-2026-60004, among other products; GreyNoise infers an overlap with Red Heron from shared infrastructure and malware, which is an inference rather than an observation. KEV lists the flaw as LAN-based, so the practical exposure is any path that reaches the switch’s management interface. That is the aviation angle: GS1900-class switches are what a contractor site office, a car-park attendant booth, a retail concession or a CCTV closet gets fitted with, they rarely appear in an asset register, and a stolen configuration is a map of every VLAN the switch carries plus the credentials to reach it.

items.title: Twenty-two flaws in Pepperl+Fuchs IO-Link masters, two at CVSS 9.8 — and the same firmware ships under Phoenix Contact and Carlo Gavazzi badges
items.content_text: CERT@VDE published VDE-2026-014 on 16 September: Pepperl+Fuchs has fixed 22 vulnerabilities in the firmware of its ICE2-8IOL and ICE3-8IOL IO-Link master modules, found by Nozomi Networks Labs researchers, with the fix in firmware 1.7.8. The two worst are CVE-2026-27546, an authentication bypass, and CVE-2026-27565, unauthenticated upload of a malicious IODD device-description file that executes shell scripts, both at CVSS 9.8. Most of the rest, CVE-2026-27547 through -27564, are command-injection, file-inclusion and authorisation flaws between 7.2 and 8.8 that lead to root-level code execution on the module; CVE-2026-27557 at 7.5 is an unauthenticated path traversal that reads the module’s SSH server private keys, and CVE-2026-27553 at 6.5 discloses password hashes. The same firmware is sold rebadged, so the exposure is wider than one vendor: Phoenix Contact IOL MA8 PN DI8 and IOL MA8 EIP DI8 masters carry 20 of the CVEs under VDE-2026-027, and Carlo Gavazzi YL212 and YN115 masters are covered by VDE-2026-028, all with the same 1.7.8 fix and the same date. No exploitation is reported and CISA has not yet republished it. Our assessment of the aviation relevance, since no airport is named: IO-Link is the sensor and actuator layer of modern conveyor and sortation systems, and baggage-handling systems are assembled by integrators from exactly this class of discrete-automation component. A master module that gives root to anyone who can reach its web interface is a foothold on the PROFINET or EtherNet/IP segment that runs the belts.
tags: Advisory — CERT@VDE VDE-2026-014; no known exploitation

items.title: Six flaws in Digital Watchdog VMAX video recorders, the top two at CVSS 9.6 — CISA lists Transportation Systems among the sectors that run them
items.content_text: CISA published ICSA-26-258-01 on 15 September covering Digital Watchdog VMAX digital and network video recorders — the A1 G4, IP G4, A1 PLUS, VA1G4 and VG4 lines. Six CVEs are listed, led by CVE-2026-66890 and CVE-2026-66887 at CVSS 9.6, with CVE-2026-68070 and CVE-2026-68950 at 8.8 and two lower-rated issues at 6.8 and 6.5. CISA states that exploitation can give an attacker full administrative control of the recorder. Updated firmware is available from the vendor, and no exploitation has been reported. The sectors CISA names for this advisory are Commercial Facilities, Government Services and Facilities, Healthcare and Public Health, and Transportation Systems. That last one is why it is carried here: recorders of this class are ordinary physical-security infrastructure in terminals, car parks, cargo sheds and landside offices, they are frequently installed and maintained by a security integrator rather than by IT, and they sit on cabling that often runs into the same closets as access control. Nothing in the advisory names an airport — treat this as an inventory question, not an aviation incident.

items.title: CISA’s 22 September batch brings nine advisories, and two of them are airport-terminal systems: Siemens Desigo CC building management and Siveillance Control security management
items.content_text: CISA released nine ICS advisories on Tuesday 22 September, ICSA-26-265-01 through -09. Two cover the lwIP embedded TCP/IP stack: an out-of-bounds write in its MQTT client application, reported by Shahriyar Jalayeri of ByteRay (-01), and a double free, reported by Eric Evenchick of Tetrel Security (-02). Six are Siemens: Siveillance Control, an unrestricted upload of a file with a dangerous type (-03); SIPLUS and SIMATIC products affected by the third-party Linux “Copy Fail” flaw (-04); the Desigo CC family, a code injection reported by Michelin CERT (-05); Industrial Edge Management, a third-party weak password-recovery issue (-06); SIMOVE Fleetmanager and SIPLANT, a relative path traversal (-07); and WTV676 and WTV776, improper validation of a specified type of input (-08). The last is OpenPLC, a cross-site scripting flaw (-09). For this page, two of those matter most. Desigo CC is Siemens’ building-management platform and sits over HVAC, fire and energy systems in many terminals. Siveillance Control is a security-management platform that brings access control, video and alarms together in a control room. We could not reach CISA’s own advisory pages at generation time. CVE numbers, CVSS scores, fix availability and CISA’s sector listings are therefore deliberately left out rather than taken from secondary digests; read each advisory before prioritising. No exploitation has been reported for anything in the batch.

items.title: CISA’s 17 September batch runs to seven new advisories plus one update — none of them aviation; the highest scores are in Mitsubishi engineering software and Schneider Modicon M340 controllers
items.content_text: CISA released seven new ICS advisories on Thursday 17 September, ICSA-26-260-01 through -07, plus one update: Bransys ELD, Mitsubishi Electric GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings, Hitachi Energy FACTS Control Platform, Schneider Electric Modicon M340 controllers and communication modules, Schneider Electric NetBotz 5 (750 and 755), ABB Ability Edgenius, and Schneider Electric PowerChute Serial Shutdown. The highest score we can verify in the batch is CVE-2026-15688 in GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings, an authentication-algorithm weakness rated CVSS 8.8 under v3.1 and 8.7 under v4.0, affecting all versions of Mitsubishi’s PLC engineering software. The Bransys advisory covers three credential-handling issues in an electronic logging device — hardcoded MQTT credentials at 7.5, cleartext transmission at 5.9 and hardcoded FTP credentials at 5.3, fixed in Android 11.00.00 and iOS 1.1.54. CISA lists Transportation Systems on that advisory, but ELDs are commercial-trucking hours-of-service devices and we are not going to stretch them into an aviation finding. CISA’s machine-readable advisory files now carry detail for four more. ICSA-26-260-04 republishes Schneider’s August 2025 advisory for CVE-2025-6625, a crafted FTP command that can deny service on Modicon M340 controllers and X80 Ethernet modules (CVSS 7.5 v3.1, 8.7 v4; M340 firmware fixed in SV3.70). ICSA-26-260-05 covers NetBotz 5 command injection CVE-2026-13336 (6.4 v3.1, 7.3 v4) and SQL injection CVE-2026-13337, fixed in 5.6.0. ICSA-26-260-06 is the Linux kernel “Copy Fail” privilege escalation CVE-2026-31431 (7.8) in ABB Edgenius gateways, fixed in 3.2.4.1. ICSA-26-260-07 is CVE-2026-13348 in PowerChute Serial Shutdown, a missing limit on authentication attempts (5.3 v3.1, 6.9 v4); CISA’s remediation text says to upgrade to version 1.6, but the same advisory also lists 1.6 as affected, so confirm the fixed build against Schneider’s own advisory. The NetBotz and PowerChute items are Schneider advisories originally dated 11 August that CISA has now republished; both products are ordinary fixtures of terminal comms rooms and energy centres, which is why an otherwise non-aviation batch is worth a look here. The Hitachi Energy advisory (-03) was still not verifiable at generation time, and its scores are deliberately omitted rather than guessed. Separately, CISA updated ICSA-26-211-07 (Mitsubishi Electric CC-Link IE TSN) on the same day, adding eight affected products. No exploitation is reported for anything in the batch.

items.title: GitLab CVSS 10 path traversal is being exploited, and airport and airline teams host more of it than they think
items.content_text: GitLab patched CVE-2026-85706 on 10 September, a path-traversal flaw in the repository commits API that it rated CVSS 10.0 and that allows an unauthenticated attacker to read arbitrary files from a GitLab server. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Friday 11 September with a remediation deadline for federal agencies of Monday 14 September. watchTowr reported it was already seeing in-the-wild probes for vulnerable servers, and Hong Kong’s CERT issued its own advisory on 14 September stating the flaw is being exploited in the wild. A second flaw fixed in the same release, CVE-2026-87719, can expose sensitive information from Enterprise Edition servers. Airport and airline estates version baggage-handling integrations, gate and stand allocation logic, BMS and access-control middleware, MRO systems and airline operations tooling in self-hosted GitLab. Unauthenticated file reads against those servers surface the service accounts and API keys that reach airside and terminal systems.

items.title: Nozomi finishes its Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 research: twelve flaws, several chainable to root on an OT edge device — patched, unexploited, and older than it looks
items.content_text: Correction to the previous edition. This entry previously read as a new critical disclosure dated 15 September. It was not. The underlying CVEs were disclosed in May 2025 under CISA advisory ICSA-25-135-18; what happened on 15 September was a CISA update to that advisory, adding the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client and vendor fixes. The research behind it published in two parts: the first, on 10 September, covered four PROFINET Discovery and basic Configuration Protocol memory-corruption flaws in the SCALANCE LPE9403 — an uninitialised value, a NULL pointer dereference and two out-of-bounds reads, each rated CVSS 5.3 and each a denial of service rather than code execution. The second part, published by Nozomi Networks Labs on 18 September, gives the full picture: twelve vulnerabilities in total, nine in the device firmware rated between 5.3 and 8.5 and three in the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client rated between 6.7 and 8.5. Nozomi demonstrated that several of them can be chained to obtain root-level control of the device, which in an OT context means manipulating telemetry, suppressing alarms, reading operational data, disrupting services and moving laterally. Affected are LPE9403 firmware below V4.0 HF0 and the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client through V2.1; Siemens has published advisories and fixes, with V4.0 HF0 and later the fixed firmware. There is no evidence of exploitation in the wild. For aviation the relevance is where these devices sit: the LPE9403 is a local-processing engine used as a PROFINET edge collector, and where an integrator has put one into baggage, plant-room, BMS or airfield equipment, root on it is root inside the segment that equipment lives in.

items.title: Moxa fixes an unauthenticated crash in the web login of its TN-4500B switches — a rolling-stock line, so the airport question is the people-mover
items.content_text: Moxa published security advisory MPSA-252620 on 18 September for CVE-2026-15579 in its TN-4500B Ethernet switch series, a line Moxa’s product page describes as designed for railway applications including rolling stock and as meeting EN 50155 test requirements. The flaw is an out-of-bounds write in the web login: the username field is not length-checked, so a remote, unauthenticated attacker who can reach the web interface can send an overlong value and crash the authentication process. Moxa describes the impact as denial of service with no confidentiality loss, scores it CVSS v4 8.8 and rates it High. Firmware v2.0 and earlier is affected; v2.1 or later fixes it. The advisory makes no statement about exploitation and we found no report of attacks. This is not an airport product and we have no evidence of it at any airport. It is carried because the one place a rolling-stock switch does turn up on an airport estate is the automated people-mover or airside shuttle, which is usually maintained by a rail systems contractor under a separate contract and separate security regime from the terminal. If you have no people-mover, file this; if you do, the question is whether the on-board network’s web management is reachable from the train-to-ground link or from the maintenance depot network.

items.title: Rockwell extends its lock-out recovery guidance to Micro820 and Micro850 — the small PLCs in the parts of an airport that never get a security review
items.content_text: Rockwell Automation revised security notice SD1790 for a fifth time on 18 September. The notice, first published on 30 July, is titled as hardening guidance and instructions for restoring access when a controller’s password is unknown, and revision 5.0 extends the recovery and hardening instructions to Micro820 and Micro850 controllers alongside the MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 it already covered. It exists because of the FBI’s public service announcement of 30 July, which described attackers remotely altering the configuration of internet-exposed PLCs, changing IP addresses and setting passwords where none had existed, locking operators out of their own controllers. There is no CVE; the guidance is to remove controllers from direct internet exposure, reach them through a VPN and firewall isolation, set strong passwords, keep offline project backups, disable the controller’s HTTP server and keep firmware current. Revision 5.0 adds no new incident data and names no sector; Rockwell has published no new vulnerability advisories since its 1 September batch. Our assessment of why it belongs here: MicroLogix and Micro800 controllers are the PLCs of small standalone plant — car-park barriers and pay-on-foot systems, pump stations, fuel-farm ancillaries, de-icing fluid recovery, packaged HVAC — typically installed by a mechanical or electrical contractor with a cellular router for remote support, and typically absent from the airport’s own asset register. The FBI’s scenario, a controller that suddenly has a password its owner does not know, is the one those sites are least prepared to recover from.

items.title: An APT cluster whose tooling overlaps Sandworm and a ransomware operator that deployed Qilin are exploiting Cisco firewall management — the boundary between airport IT and airfield OT
items.content_text: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center is being exploited in the wild. The flaw is a critical authentication bypass caused by an improper system process created at boot; a remote, unauthenticated attacker sends crafted HTTP requests and gains root on the underlying operating system. Cisco patched it in early March and added indicators of compromise in late July, then disclosed on 9 September that it had observed exploitation from August. CISA added the CVE to its KEV catalog with a 12 September federal deadline, which has now passed. Cisco Talos tracks three post-compromise clusters across this flaw and the earlier static-credential flaw CVE-2026-20316: UAT-12197, unattributed, which used CVE-2026-20079 to plant a web shell and a JAR-based command executor and exfiltrate credentials; UAT-11823, an APT that used both CVEs and is Sandworm-linked through tooling overlap, deploying a Cyclops Blink variant — Talos does not say Sandworm itself carried it out; and UAT-11988, which Talos assesses with high confidence to be a ransomware operator with TTPs consistent with Qilin affiliates, came in through CVE-2026-20316 alone, enumerated targets for encryption and deployed Qilin on selected endpoints. CVE-2026-20316 is not in the KEV catalogue. On 16 September Cisco shipped its September hardening release for ASA, FTD and FMC (CVE-2026-20329 to CVE-2026-20336, maximum CVSS 9.9), which accompanies the exploited FMC flaws. Airports should treat this as an airfield-and-terminal segmentation problem rather than an office IT patch. The firewalls FMC configures are usually what stands between the corporate network and baggage handling, jet bridges, fuelling, de-icing, airfield lighting, BMS and access control.

items.title: ScreenConnect is being used to push scripts to endpoints as they connect — the console your handlers and integrators already have on your estate
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-84869 in ConnectWise ScreenConnect to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 12 September with a federal remediation deadline of 14 September. The flaw is a missing authorisation check rated CVSS 9.9 that permits unauthorised file transfer and code execution, and three separate incidents have been documented in which threat actors abused it to push malicious scripts to endpoints as those endpoints newly connected to a server. That detail is the one that matters operationally: the malicious action arrives through the legitimate management channel, signed off by the tool the estate is built to trust, so it looks like maintenance rather than intrusion. ScreenConnect and its peers are the standing path by which ground handlers, baggage and BMS maintainers, access-control contractors and airport systems integrators reach terminal systems out of hours, frequently on instances the airport authority neither owns nor patches. It sits alongside this week’s other confirmed remote-access exploitation as a single theme: the attacker is no longer forcing a boundary, they are borrowing the support tool that already crosses it.

items.title: NetScaler is being probed harder than it is being patched — 56 exploitation attempts in a week against an authentication bypass now in KEV
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-19490 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 9 September, an authentication bypass rated CVSS 9.3 affecting Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway in AAA virtual server and Gateway configurations, with a federal deadline of 12 September that has now passed. Honeypot telemetry logged 56 exploitation attempts from 3 September onward, 36 of them on 8 September alone, which is the shape of opportunistic mass scanning rather than targeted intrusion — internet-facing devices are being found and tried before their owners finish the change window. It arrived in the same KEV batch as the Fortinet FortiOS, FortiSwitchManager and FortiSASE heap overflow CVE-2025-25249, exploited since July and linked to a campaign that has infected an estimated 178 FortiGate devices with the PivotC2 remote access trojan. Aviation reads these as one exposure. NetScaler Gateway is a common front door for airline crew and operations portals, engineering and MRO applications and third-party access into terminal systems, and FortiGate is among the most common devices sitting on the boundary between an airport’s corporate network and its airside estate. An authentication bypass on either is not a data-theft problem, it is a segmentation problem.

items.title: MikroTik RouterOS “MikroTrick” chain moves from disclosed to confirmed exploited — CERT Polska
items.content_text: CERT Polska issued an alert on 9 September confirming that the MikroTik RouterOS vulnerabilities known as the “MikroTrick” chain — previously disclosed but not confirmed exploited — are now being used in real-world attacks, with activity observed since at least 2 September. The chain pairs an SSH authentication-bypass flaw, CVE-2026-67276 at CVSS 9.2, with an SSH privilege-escalation flaw, CVE-2026-86060 also at CVSS 9.2, to take full unauthenticated administrative control of an internet-exposed RouterOS device; a third bug, CVE-2026-67277, allows memory disclosure or denial of service through the bandwidth-test service. CERT Polska named no victims and no sectors, noting only that MikroTik hardware is widely deployed across ISPs, data centres, enterprises and critical-infrastructure networks. That breadth is the aviation relevance rather than any confirmed airport targeting: RouterOS boxes turn up in the inexpensive, quietly-installed corners of an airport estate — remote stands and cargo sheds, car parks and shuttle depots, contractor site offices, CCTV and Wi-Fi backhaul — the places least likely to appear in an asset register and most likely to have an SSH port open for vendor support.

items.title: CISA adds four exploited flaws on 8 September, led by a CVSS 10 pre-auth RCE in the remote-monitoring platform many airport contractors run on
items.content_text: The 8 September KEV batch is headed by CVE-2026-86218 in N-able N-central, a static code-injection flaw rated CVSS 10.0 that gives unauthenticated remote code execution. N-able has confirmed exploitation in the wild, Huntress observed attacks against the platform’s API and appliance logs from 4 September, and the vendor shipped 2026.3 Hotfix 4 on 5 September — its fourth hotfix in five weeks. Federal agencies have until 11 September. Also added: two Windows zero-days confirmed exploited on the same day, CVE-2026-81963 in the Update Stack and CVE-2026-85880 in ALPC, both giving SYSTEM, plus CVE-2026-75650 in Adobe Commerce. N-central matters here because it is a managed-service platform: at airports it is the sort of console an integrator uses to reach terminal building management, access control and baggage estates.

items.title: September ICS Patch Tuesday: Siemens fixes an authentication bypass in protection relays, Schneider a critical flaw in Modicon M580
items.content_text: Siemens published nine advisories, seven of them on 8 September. The heaviest is SSA-142885 covering Reyrolle 7SR5 protection and control relays: fourteen CVEs in all versions before V2.70, led by CVE-2026-62645 at CVSS 9.8, where the web interface leaks enough information for an attacker to calculate current and past session identifiers and bypass authentication. Critical items also landed in Industrial Edge Management, Open Interface Services and SIMOVE Fleetmanager. Schneider Electric issued four advisories the same day, the most severe a critical authentication flaw in Modicon M580 and M580 Safety controllers, CVE-2026-3869 at CVSS 9.2, with high-severity fixes for PowerLogic T300 and EcoStruxure IT Data Center Expert. Aveva patched four flaws in Pipeline Integrity Monitor, and CISA picked that one up separately on 10 September as ICSA-26-253-01: hard-coded cryptographic key CVE-2026-81821 and weak password hashing CVE-2026-81822, both CVSS 8.4, plus a missing-authorisation flaw at 5.3 and a cross-site scripting flaw at 4.7, in versions up to and including 2025 SP1 P1, fixed in the 2025 SP1 P2 security update. No exploitation has been reported for any of it.

items.title: CISA and FBI on integrator risk: one compromised automation vendor, about 800 files of its customers’ SCADA details — and transportation among those customers
items.content_text: CISA and the FBI published a joint fact sheet on 24 September, Considerations for Critical Infrastructure Operators Working with Third-Party ICS Integrators. It cites a case in which foreign cyber actors, between March and April 2025, compromised a US industrial automation company that provided system integration, engineering consulting and SCADA programming services to customers including power utilities and transportation entities. On the integrator’s network the actors searched for terms including “customers” and “SCADA” and packaged approximately 800 files — customer SCADA information, ICS device details and schematics — into nine archive files. The fact sheet names neither the integrator, its customers nor the actor, and describes no disruption. Its recommendations are least privilege for every integrator connection, on-demand remote access that the operator authorises and can monitor, and contract terms covering data storage, remote access and patching. No airport, airline or air navigation service provider is named, and this is guidance, not a new incident. It is carried here because airport ground OT is among the most integrator-dependent estates in transport: baggage handling, jet bridges, airfield lighting, fuel systems and terminal BMS are typically installed and supported by a specialist integrator who holds the drawings, the configurations and a standing way in — the same asset class the 2025 case shows is worth stealing even when the operator’s own network is never touched.

items.title: CISA’s Cyber Storm X ran a nation-state scenario against transportation, but the published scope names rail and ports, not aviation
items.content_text: CISA announced on 22 September that it had hosted Cyber Storm X, the latest in its national cyber exercise series. The four-day exercise brought together about 2,000 participants from more than 200 federal, state, local and private-sector organisations. The scenario was a nation-state adversary targeting the Transportation Systems sector, specifically rail and ports, and the Water and Wastewater Systems sector. Acting CISA Director Nick Andersen said the series “helps critical infrastructure owners and operators understand how we would manage a large-scale cyber incident.” CISA will produce a public after-action report of observations, analysis and recommendations. The published coverage gives no exact exercise dates. Aviation is not named in the scope. That is itself useful to know, because it means the national playbook tested this month was not rehearsed against an airport or airline scenario. The after-action report is still worth reading when it appears, because cross-sector coordination, information sharing and the federal-to-operator handoff are the same whichever mode of transport is attacked.

items.title: CISA publishes a cyber-decoys guide — the rare detection control you can add to an airport network without touching what it controls
items.content_text: CISA released “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” on 17 September. The guide defines decoys as assets that look like legitimate systems, accounts or data but exist to distract an adversary, reveal their presence, or collect intelligence on how they operate, and it sets out three phases: preparation, execution and analysis. CISA positions the technique alongside Zero Trust rather than as a replacement for it. The reason it reads well for aviation is the constraint every airport security team knows: you cannot install an agent on a baggage controller, a jet-bridge PLC or an airfield-lighting panel, and a change window on those systems is expensive. A decoy is additive — a fake engineering workstation, a planted credential that no legitimate process should ever use, a file share named to look like integrator documentation — and it produces a signal with almost no false positives, because nothing legitimate should touch it. The catch is that a decoy nobody monitors is decoration, so the alerting path matters more than the decoy.

items.title: CISA is retiring its weekly vulnerability bulletin on 28 September — a small change that breaks a lot of quiet Monday-morning routines
items.content_text: CISA will stop publishing its weekly Vulnerability Summary bulletin from 28 September, pointing readers instead to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, its alerts and its advisories. The agency frames the move as consistent with the risk-based prioritisation set out in binding operational directive BOD 26-04 of June 2026: a weekly digest of everything published is a poor instrument next to a catalog of what is actually being exploited. Nothing in the reporting indicates the ICS advisory stream is affected. It is worth flagging for aviation readers because the weekly bulletin is quietly load-bearing in small vulnerability-management routines — the airport or airline team without a dedicated threat-intel function that reads one email a week and triages from it. If that describes your process, the replacement is not a new email; it is a subscription to KEV and the ICS advisory feed, and a decision about who reads them and how often.

items.title: A US rule now counts a cyberattack as a “not controllable” cause of delay — and ties the relief to being compliant
items.content_text: A Department of Transportation rule reported on 11 September creates a new cause-of-delay category and designates ten types of disruption as “not controllable,” cyberattacks among them. Where a carrier is compliant with the cybersecurity regulations that apply to it, it no longer owes meals, hotels or comparable amenities under its customer service plan when one of those causes grounds flights; carriers that are not compliant remain subject to the requirements. Nothing here touches an aviation control system — this is advisory-only for OT. What it changes is the cost calculus behind a grounding cyber incident, and it puts a financial edge on being able to evidence compliance, because the carrier that can show it met its obligations is the one that keeps the relief. Reporting places the rule against the backdrop of the Scattered Spider intrusions at airlines, the Collins Aerospace incident that delayed European flights and the 2024 CrowdStrike outage, and notes there is no formal accounting of how often cyberattacks previously triggered compensation claims. Carried here factually as a regulatory change, with no comment on the policy debate around it.

items.title: ENISA switches on the Single Reporting Platform as the Cyber Resilience Act’s vulnerability reporting duties take effect
items.content_text: The EU Agency for Cybersecurity deployed the initial operating capability of its Single Reporting Platform, announced 14 September, giving manufacturers and open-source software stewards the channel they need to meet Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations that took effect this month. Under the CRA, makers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents on a defined clock, with an early warning followed by a fuller notification. Airports and airlines are mostly beneficiaries here, but suppliers of baggage, BMS, access-control and airfield equipment placing products on the EU market now carry an active-exploitation reporting duty with a hard clock on it. Reported here factually as a regulatory milestone, without comment on the underlying policy debate.
